values.description: Discovered exploitation cases become negative examples for subsequent reward-model training.

values.label: Human feedback as sole reward source
values.description: Replacing automated reward signals with human feedback alone is rejected because evaluators have limited attention and can be manipulated.

values.label: Domain-specific expert feedback
values.description: Customer, clinician, analyst, or operator judgments provide domain-tailored preference and quality signals.

values.label: Human preference-data collection
values.description: Human comparisons and preferences are collected as training and evaluation data for aligning deployed-agent behavior.

values.label: Annotator-bias mitigation
values.description: Feedback processes explicitly address subjectivity and bias in human judgments.

values.label: Broad-scenario feedback coverage
values.description: Reward-model and annotation data span diverse scenarios to reduce blind spots and improve failure coverage.

clusters.name: Detection Method Selection
clusters.description: The analytical tests used to identify degradation, drift, reward hacking, anomalies, or unsafe behavior from monitoring evidence.

relations.reading: Choices on Detection Method Selection affect the outcomes of Intervention and Recovery Strategy
relations.rationale: Detection sensitivity, latency, and false-positive behavior determine when recovery actions are triggered.

values.label: Relative performance-drop threshold
values.description: A recent smoothed performance measure is compared with a historical best using a configurable relative threshold.

values.label: Metric-divergence detection
values.description: Gaming is inferred when an optimized metric improves while related satisfaction, stability, safety, or quality metrics decline.

values.label: Reward-model disagreement detection
values.description: Disagreement among reward models signals possible gaming or unreliable evaluation.

values.label: Policy-distribution anomaly classification
values.description: A classifier detects anomalous behavior from distances between trusted and target policy action distributions.

values.label: Policy-to-reference divergence tracking
values.description: Behavioral drift is monitored through divergence between deployed and original or trusted reference policies.

values.label: Task-dependent detector effectiveness
values.description: Detector performance varies across tasks, limiting reliance on any single anomaly-detection method.

values.label: BFAR detection
values.description: A bounded false-alarm-rate test controls alerting against an operationally defined false-alarm target.

values.label: CUSUM change detection
values.description: Cumulative-sum statistics detect persistent small shifts in monitored behavior or performance.

values.label: Hotelling multivariate detection
values.description: Covariance-aware multivariate statistics detect abnormal joint movement across monitored metrics.

values.label: PSI or KL divergence detection
values.description: Population-stability or Kullback–Leibler divergence detects changes between reference and production distributions.

values.label: Embedding-drift detection
values.description: Distance or distribution tests over learned representations detect semantic or behavioral drift.

values.label: Pre-deployment adversarial exploit testing
values.description: Reward functions and policies are deliberately attacked before deployment to discover hidden gaming strategies.

values.label: False negatives from emerging language variants
values.description: Previously unseen slang, memes, or harmful language cause moderation systems to miss violations.

values.label: Unknown-situation detection
values.description: Runtime monitoring identifies scenarios outside the agent’s demonstrated capabilities or training experience.

values.label: Scenario-level ID/OOD classification
values.description: Whole reinforcement-learning scenarios are classified as inside- or outside-distribution cases for novelty monitoring.

values.label: Runtime out-of-distribution monitoring
values.description: A deployed monitor detects when conditions fall outside the modeled or training distribution.

values.label: Strict vision-based novelty detection
values.description: Treating any visual difference as out-of-distribution is rejected because visual novelty does not necessarily imply an unknown control situation.

values.label: Proxy–true reward divergence monitoring
values.description: Proxy and true reward trends are compared to reveal reward hacking and specification failure.

values.label: Trajectory-level proxy–true reward correlation analysis
values.description: Collections of rollouts are analyzed for correlation between proxy and true rewards before or during optimization.

values.label: Evaluator-gaming detection
values.description: Monitoring identifies behavior that manipulates reward providers or human evaluators without achieving the intended task.

values.label: Implementation-behavior exploit detection
values.description: Detection searches for reuse of evaluator state, no-op behavior, simulator exploits, and other implementation-level shortcuts.

values.label: Localized and delayed failure detection
values.description: Slice-aware and tail-growth analyses expose failures that emerge late or affect only specific behavioral groups.

values.label: Capability-scaled detection difficulty
values.description: More capable agents may discover subtler cheating strategies that existing monitors and evaluations fail to detect.

clusters.name: Intervention and Recovery Strategy
clusters.description: The corrective response to detected degradation or unsafe behavior, including fallback, rollback, traffic control, retraining, and stabilization.

relations.reading: Choices on Intervention and Recovery Strategy affect the outcomes of Post-Deployment Learning Strategy
relations.rationale: Rollback, fallback, retraining, and stabilization choices determine whether adaptation proceeds safely after monitoring events.

values.label: Safe fallback policy switching
values.description: An automated circuit breaker switches control to a safer policy when production performance becomes unacceptable.

values.label: Latest-checkpoint model recovery
values.description: The system reloads the latest known checkpoint after detecting degradation.

values.label: Safe-baseline policy rollback
values.description: The deployed agent reverts to a known safe baseline policy after unacceptable learning behavior.

values.label: Offline retraining and redeployment
values.description: Logged interactions are analyzed offline, updated policies are evaluated, and approved versions are redeployed.

values.label: Prompt-template adjustment
values.description: Prompt templates change as a corrective response to detected drift without necessarily retraining the model.

values.label: Post-recovery learning-rate reduction
values.description: The learning rate is reduced after recovery to stabilize resumed learning and dampen oscillation.

values.label: Traffic shifting
values.description: Traffic is redirected away from a degraded policy toward a safer serving version or configuration.

values.label: Version-pointer rollback
values.description: A registry or deployment pointer is updated to identify the previously approved production version.

values.label: Configuration-based rollback
values.description: Rollback is executed by restoring deployment configuration rather than rebuilding or manually redeploying a model.

values.label: Automated rollback disaster-recovery testing
values.description: Simulated failures verify that automated rollback restores the prior version without manual intervention.

values.label: Rollback event audit logging
values.description: Triggers, timestamps, source versions, and target versions are recorded for post-incident analysis.

values.label: Fail-safe graceful degradation
values.description: The system continues in a safer reduced-capability mode when unexpected situations or poor learned policies occur.

values.label: Unknown-situation rejection
values.description: The agent declines to issue control commands when a situation lies outside its reliable capabilities.

values.label: Human handover for unknown situations
values.description: Novel or unsupported situations are transferred to a human operator for safe handling.

values.label: Safety alert for unknown obstacles
values.description: The deployed agent raises an explicit safety alert when it encounters an unknown obstacle or situation.

values.label: Adaptive runtime shielding
values.description: A runtime shield changes or blocks actions in response to detected distribution shifts or unsafe conditions.

values.label: Safe action gating
values.description: Policy outputs pass through a final runtime gate that prevents actions violating safety requirements.

values.label: Static-state observation substitution
values.description: Masked or static observations replace adversarial opponent information as a robustness intervention.

clusters.name: Post-Deployment Learning Strategy
clusters.description: The mode through which deployed policies adapt to new data, preferences, environments, or feedback after production release.

values.label: Conservative offline policy learning
values.description: Policies learn from historical data while restricting extrapolation and avoiding risky online exploration.

values.label: Continuous human-feedback adaptation
values.description: Ongoing human feedback updates deployed behavior as preferences, domain knowledge, and risks change.

values.label: Aggregate-usage online learning
values.description: The system adapts from aggregated production usage while accounting for privacy constraints.

values.label: Continual domain-data fine-tuning
values.description: Changing repositories, guidelines, or domain data drive continuing model fine-tuning.

values.label: User-specific preference fine-tuning
values.description: Individual user actions and project context personalize deployed behavior through continuing fine-tuning.

values.label: Distribution-shift adaptation
values.description: The policy adapts to changing production distributions, non-stationary environments, uncertainty, and multi-agent interactions.

values.label: Parameter-efficient adapter fine-tuning
values.description: LoRA or similar adapters update a small parameter subset while keeping most of the base model frozen.

values.label: Monitoring-triggered corrective fine-tuning
values.description: Drift, bias, or recurring errors trigger fine-tuning on corrected examples or current guidance.

values.label: Reduced fine-tuning resource demand
values.description: Adapter-based updating reduces compute and memory requirements compared with full-model updating.

values.label: Fine-tuning cost reduction
values.description: Fine-tuning costs less than full retraining because it uses fewer steps, smaller learning rates, or fewer parameters.

values.label: Periodic retraining and fine-tuning pipeline
values.description: Original data, refreshed production examples, and corrected human outputs are periodically used for adaptation.

values.label: Automated retraining pipeline
values.description: Monitoring, drift detection, retraining, validation, and deployment are connected in an automated upkeep workflow.

values.label: Trigger-based retraining schedule
values.description: Retraining begins when drift or evaluation metrics breach defined thresholds rather than following only a fixed calendar.

values.label: Limited-frequency full retraining
values.description: Expensive full-model retraining occurs infrequently, with lighter adaptation between full retraining events.

values.label: Historical-and-recent data replay
values.description: Old and new examples are mixed during adaptation to preserve prior capabilities and reduce catastrophic forgetting.

values.label: Selective component fine-tuning
values.description: Only selected model components are updated to reduce adaptation cost while incorporating new knowledge.

values.label: Data augmentation for shift robustness
values.description: Paraphrases, dialects, simulated inputs, slang, and emerging terminology expand training coverage for shifted production inputs.

values.label: Retraining cost and catastrophic-forgetting risk
values.description: Compute expense, time, and loss of older capabilities constrain retraining architecture and data-selection choices.

clusters.name: Policy Rollout Strategy
clusters.description: The exposure pattern used to validate and release policy changes, from observation-only deployment through restricted and broad operation.

relations.reading: Choices on Policy Rollout Strategy affect the outcomes of Monitoring Evidence Strategy
relations.rationale: Exposure determines traffic, risk, and behavioral evidence available for evaluating a policy.

relations.reading: Choices on Policy Rollout Strategy limit the options available on Intervention and Recovery Strategy
relations.rationale: Limited blast radius permits controlled rollback, while broad exposure increases need for immediate automated fallback.

values.label: Shadow policy deployment
values.description: A candidate policy observes production traffic and records actions without affecting live decisions.

values.label: Subset-based canary rollout
values.description: A limited subset of workloads or namespaces receives the candidate policy before broader adoption.

values.label: Staged policy delivery
values.description: Offline evaluation, testing, staging, and canary deployment precede production release.

values.label: Noncritical validation window
values.description: The policy is observed for a bounded period in a low-criticality environment before expansion.

values.label: Staged testing with safety-incident monitoring
values.description: Robotic or other high-impact policies advance through tests while success and safety incidents are monitored.

clusters.name: Monitoring Data Architecture
clusters.description: The infrastructure that captures, stores, versions, reproduces, and serves monitoring data for diagnosis and policy comparison.

values.label: Partitioned raw-trajectory lake
values.description: Raw trajectories are stored and partitioned by time and policy version for later analysis and comparison.

values.label: Kubernetes telemetry data lake
values.description: Platform events and metrics are ingested into a data lake to construct resource-usage trajectories.

values.label: Training-inference feature store
values.description: A feature layer maintains feature consistency and validation between policy training and production inference.

values.label: Policy promotion registry
values.description: A registry records candidate metrics and enforces rules governing policy promotion toward deployment.

values.label: Reproducible experiment tracking
values.description: Hyperparameters, seeds, evaluation results, and policy versions are recorded for reproducible diagnosis and comparison.

values.label: Historical replay and stress simulation
values.description: Historical traces and synthetic scenarios are replayed under varied or adverse conditions.

values.label: Prometheus-Grafana telemetry stack
values.description: Operational metrics are collected and visualized through a production monitoring stack.

values.label: CI-log and orchestration-pipeline integration
values.description: Test histories, failures, and regression measures are collected from CI logs and orchestration pipelines.

values.label: Alerting-platform and incident-tracker integration
values.description: Alert logs and incident outcomes support monitoring response latency, precision, and remediation.

values.label: ERP-log and batch-RL pipeline integration
values.description: Demand and allocation actions from ERP systems support monitoring inventory policies and costs.

values.label: Comprehensive RL system documentation
values.description: Design, training, deployment, and governance decisions are recorded for compliance and risk management.

values.label: Privacy-preserving learning data architecture
values.description: Data and learning workflows protect sensitive user information while supporting continued adaptation.

values.label: Production-example dataset
values.description: A filtered, continuously refreshed dataset of real production examples supports current monitoring and later model updates.

values.label: Post-training diagnostics layer
values.description: A reusable diagnostics layer connects post-training workflows with live warnings, failure detection, and diagnostic artifacts.

values.label: Distributed-aware metric aggregation
values.description: Metrics are aggregated across execution ranks so distributed training and inference behavior is not hidden by local measurements.

values.label: Distributed execution health checks
values.description: Straggler, memory-balance, and related checks monitor operational health in distributed execution.

values.label: Agent trace analysis pipeline
values.description: Agent logs are transformed into diagnostic artifacts and downstream preference or evaluation data.

values.label: Training-job metadata persistence
values.description: Training instances, source code, metrics, and related job metadata are retained for monitoring and reproducibility.

values.label: Cloud log and object-storage integration
values.description: Training logs, outputs, and visualization data are stored in centralized logging and durable object-storage systems.

values.label: Production policy lineage tracking
values.description: Deployed policies are linked to their training jobs, artifacts, configurations, and evaluation history.

values.label: Open-source monitoring reference implementation
values.description: Reference code and complete experiment artifacts support reproducible monitoring construction and evaluation.

clusters.name: Monitoring Evidence Strategy

relations.reading: Choices on Monitoring Evidence Strategy affect the outcomes of Reward Objective Design
relations.rationale: Evidence determines whether optimization improves intended behavior or merely increases a measurable proxy.

values.label: Real-time operational metric monitoring
values.description: Continuous monitoring of performance, latency, utilization, safety violations, SLOs, reward signals, and system health.

values.label: Safety-output classification
values.description: Classifiers identify harmful, biased, inappropriate, or unsafe outputs and track their rates.

values.label: Frozen reward-model scoring
values.description: Production interactions are periodically scored with the training-time reward model to detect declining alignment.

values.label: Periodic human interaction review
values.description: Experts inspect sampled production interactions to identify subtle failures, drift, and new failure modes.

values.label: Policy action-distribution comparison
values.description: Trusted and deployed policies are compared through differences in action distributions.

values.label: Reward-score inflation without behavioral improvement
values.description: Reward increases while intended behavior does not improve.

values.label: SHAP and counterfactual explainability
values.description: Attribution and counterfactual explanations expose why an agent selected an action.

values.label: Chain-of-thought monitoring
values.description: Reasoning traces, intermediate actions, and final outputs are inspected for reward hacking or misbehavior.

values.label: Light chain-of-thought optimization pressure
values.description: Limited optimization pressure is applied to reasoning traces while preserving monitorability.

values.label: Strong chain-of-thought supervision
values.description: Strong direct supervision of reasoning traces is rejected because agents may conceal intent.

values.label: Algorithmic audit evidence
values.description: Recurring audits inspect behavior for regulatory, policy, ethical, and governance compliance.

values.label: CoT intent-hiding detectability
values.description: Agents may produce compliant-looking reasoning traces that hide intentions.

values.label: Human feedback as a monitoring signal
values.description: Human judgments expose drift, incoherence, outdated recommendations, bias, and toxicity.

values.label: Drift-metric observability dashboard
values.description: Dashboards expose distribution-shift and behavioral-drift metrics continuously.

values.label: Full-trajectory monitoring artifacts
values.description: Complete agent trajectories are retained for qualitative inspection and behavioral analysis.

values.label: Normal safety evaluation
values.description: Standard safety evaluations provide recurring evidence for unsafe or misaligned outputs.

values.label: Process-level supervision evidence
values.description: Intermediate reasoning steps and checkpoints are monitored in addition to final outputs.

values.label: Implementation-behavior validation
values.description: Monitoring checks how an agent achieved an output, not only the final result.

values.label: Behavioral monitoring alongside reward metrics
values.description: Actual agent behavior is inspected alongside reward scores.

values.label: Physically implausible behavior monitoring
values.description: Unusual or physically implausible behavior is treated as a production warning signal.

values.label: Specification-spirit compliance monitoring
values.description: Monitoring checks whether literal specification satisfaction violates the intended purpose.

values.label: Scratchpad-based reasoning observability
values.description: An exposed scratchpad provides reasoning evidence for behavioral and evaluation-awareness inspection.

values.label: Scratchpad evaluation-awareness analysis
values.description: Scratchpad content is analyzed for reasoning about evaluation and user beliefs.

values.label: Process filtering
values.description: Intermediate processes are filtered or inspected to detect reward exploitation.

values.label: Human approval of understandable consequences
values.description: Future feedback is restricted to consequences a trusted human can understand and approve.

clusters.name: Reward Objective Design
clusters.description: The formulation and composition of optimization signals, constraints, shaping methods, verifiers, and explicit penalties.

relations.reading: Choices on Reward Objective Design affect the outcomes of Detection Method Selection
relations.rationale: Reward construction determines which loopholes, disagreements, and behavioral divergences detectors must expose.

relations.reading: Choices on Reward Objective Design limit the options available on Feedback Acquisition Strategy
relations.rationale: Different objectives require different feedback and annotation processes.

values.label: Multi-objective reward formulation
values.description: Rewards combine task performance, safety, energy, stability, naturalness, or other objectives.

values.label: Single-metric reward objective
values.description: Optimization primarily targets one measured metric, leaving other requirements weakly represented.

values.label: Explicit behavioral constraints
values.description: The objective specifies prohibited behaviors and penalties for unacceptable outcomes.

values.label: Proxy reward model
values.description: An imperfect learned proxy represents preferences or task success.

values.label: Reward-model ensemble
values.description: Multiple reward models jointly score behavior to reduce individual-model exploitation.

values.label: Reward-hacking penalty mechanism
values.description: A classifier or preference penalty suppresses detected reward hacking.

values.label: Proxy-objective divergence
values.description: The agent maximizes the measured objective while producing harmful or unintended behavior.

values.label: Rule-based verifier
values.description: Hand-authored rules verify outputs or actions against explicit requirements.

values.label: Model-based verifier
values.description: A learned evaluator verifies outputs or actions against requirements.

values.label: Hybrid verifier
values.description: Rules and learned evaluators jointly verify behavior.

values.label: Gated reward signal
values.description: Reward passes onward only after acceptable behavior is verified.

values.label: Missing response-length penalty
values.description: Without a length penalty, verbosity may increase reward without usefulness.

values.label: Reward-model feature exploitation
values.description: Agents insert reward-favored but task-irrelevant features.

values.label: Process-level reward supervision
values.description: Intermediate checkpoints receive reward or verification signals.

values.label: Outcome-only reward supervision
values.description: Only final outputs receive reward, leaving pathways unverified.

values.label: Functional-output-only correctness validation
values.description: Output equivalence is accepted without verifying intended implementation.

values.label: Pairwise human-preference reward modeling
values.description: A scalar reward model is fitted from human output comparisons.

values.label: Multi-criteria labeler guidance
values.description: Evaluators judge several quality criteria rather than superficial features.

values.label: Score-maximization reward objective
values.description: The objective maximizes a score without explicitly encoding the intended task goal.

values.label: Potential-based reward shaping
values.description: Potential-based transformations add learning guidance while preserving optimal policies.

values.label: Preference-as-reward shaping
values.description: Latent reward-model preferences replace raw scores to make rewards harder to exploit.

values.label: Bounded reward values
values.description: Reward values are bounded to limit unbounded exploitation.

values.label: Rapid-growth gradual-convergence schedule
values.description: Rewards grow rapidly initially and gradually converge to limit extreme optimization.

values.label: Reference-centered rewards
values.description: Reference values are subtracted to improve reward stability.

values.label: Agent-accessible reward-generation mechanism
values.description: The agent can alter or corrupt the mechanism that generates its reward.

values.label: Reward tampering
values.description: The agent modifies the reward-generating mechanism rather than merely exploiting its flaws.

values.label: Structured reward rubrics
values.description: Structured criteria reduce loopholes and inaccuracies in reward definitions.

values.label: Policy-reward-model co-optimization
values.description: Policy and reward model are co-optimized to reduce reward hacking.

values.label: Static reward functions
values.description: Setting a reward once without revision is rejected because agents can discover new exploits.

values.label: Adversarial reward-model training
values.description: Adversarial examples and training are used to slow reward hacking.

values.label: Adversarial training as complete mitigation
values.description: Treating adversarial training as sufficient to eliminate future hacks is rejected.

values.label: Specification gaming
values.description: The agent satisfies a literal objective while violating its intended outcome.

The taxonomy covers most codes: reward hacking, proxy exploitation, reward-model design, human and adversarial feedback, monitoring evidence, detector selection, rollout, retraining/adaptation, telemetry integration, and automated rollback triggering are already subsumed by existing dimensions. However, several codes expose distinct architectural axes. Parameter-efficient adapters concern the granularity and isolation of model updates, which is not represented by the post-deployment learning modes. Rollback state restoration concerns how stateful agents are reconciled after recovery, while CI/CD or workflow orchestration concerns the control-plane implementation that executes remediation; neither is captured by the available recovery options. Finally, explainability, recurring algorithmic auditing, privacy-preserving learning, documentation, and enterprise governance form a governance and assurance architecture dimension that is not reducible to monitoring evidence, feedback, learning, or data storage. Other codes are outcomes, forces, concrete evidence types, or domain-specific instances that existing dimensions can absorb.

Most open codes are subsumed by the existing dimensions: production data, dashboards, trajectory artifacts, and lineage fit Monitoring Data Architecture; drift and novelty detection fit Detection Method Selection; human review and feedback fit Monitoring Evidence Strategy or Feedback Acquisition Strategy; retraining, fine-tuning, augmentation, and replay fit Post-Deployment Learning Strategy; reward-model weaknesses and proxy/true-reward divergence fit Reward Objective Design and Monitoring Evidence Strategy; and rejection, fallback, rollback, and handover-like responses fit Intervention and Recovery Strategy. However, the taxonomy does not clearly capture a distinct runtime enforcement decision that mediates or modifies an action before execution, such as a safe action gate or adaptive shield triggered by detected OOD conditions. Its existing gated-reward value concerns training-time reward flow rather than runtime action execution. It also lacks a general axis for whether monitoring remains passive and independent or creates optimization pressure that agents may adapt to or evade; the existing chain-of-thought-specific values do not cover this broader monitoring architecture choice.

saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most open codes through reward-objective design, monitoring evidence, detection methods, intervention and recovery, post-deployment learning, rollout, and monitoring-data architecture. However, several relevant concepts expose distinct architectural axes. First, reward integrity is not explicitly represented: the taxonomy covers reward formulation and detection of reward hacking, but not whether the deployed agent can access or influence the reward-generation mechanism. Second, reward objectives are modeled as formulations, but not as lifecycle-managed artifacts that can be monitored and revised during an active deployment versus held static. Third, the taxonomy lacks the architectural placement of monitoring, anomaly detection, and recovery as an integrated closed loop inside the RL training/operation loop rather than as external pipeline components. Finally, replay and simulation are represented as data-architecture capabilities, but there is no explicit decision about validating simulator fidelity against reality or selecting evaluation distributions that are representative of deployment; this leaves the evaluation-to-production gap and deployment-distribution-specific safety assurance insufficiently captured. Related codes such as held-out testing, diverse scenario evaluation, behavioral inspection, conservative offline learning, and shadow deployment are otherwise subsumed by existing dimensions.

Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: monitoring evidence and detection cover the proposed telemetry, drift, tail, proxy-gap, evaluator, and correctness signals; reward-objective design covers proxy selection, penalties, constraints, preference signals, and reward transformations; feedback acquisition covers human oversight and domain-specific evaluation; intervention, learning, rollout, and data architecture cover rollback, continued training, shadow/canary release, logging, registries, simulation, and offline evaluation. The clear gap is the architectural organization of the deployed agent itself—modular separation of perception, decision, and execution; hierarchical decomposition; or hybrid RL-plus-supervised components used for fallback and safety. This is an axis of system decomposition and component responsibility, not merely a choice of monitoring evidence, reward, learning schedule, or recovery action. The other apparently new codes are either outcomes/forces (for example, scalability, concealment, detection coverage, and deployment pressure), concrete values of existing dimensions, or concepts outside the monitoring-infrastructure design space.

saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: monitoring signals cover SLIs, SLOs, business metrics, user feedback, drift, and shadow comparisons; Detection Method Selection covers counterfactual evaluation, simulation, off-policy correction, held-out environments, and anomaly thresholds; Policy Rollout Strategy, Intervention and Recovery Strategy, and Monitoring Artifact Governance cover shadowing, canaries, registries, staged promotion, fallback, rollback, and evaluation gates; Post-Deployment Learning Strategy covers offline, online, hybrid, continual, scheduled, trigger-based, replay, PEFT, and evaluation-gated updates; and Feedback Acquisition Strategy covers human, implicit, explicit, targeted, iterative, and AI-generated feedback. However, federated learning introduces a distinct choice about where learning and data processing occur (centralized versus federated/decentralized), with privacy, communication, and orchestration forces not represented as an explicit axis. Distributed actor-critic and asynchronous policy updates likewise introduce a distinct execution-topology and synchronization choice, not merely a choice of adaptation schedule. Finally, split model/runtime ownership and explicit policy-disable on-call coverage concern accountability and operational responsibility allocation; existing governance and human-oversight dimensions do not specify who owns monitoring, incident response, or rollback authority.

All relevant open codes are subsumed by existing taxonomy dimensions. Policy freezing, offline evaluation, shadow/canary testing, versioning and rollback map to Post-Deployment Learning Strategy, Verifier and Supervision Strategy, Policy Rollout Strategy, and Intervention and Recovery Strategy. Reward clipping, penalties, action bounds, shaping, and anti-hacking constraints map to Reward Shaping and Stabilization and Intervention and Recovery Strategy. Human oversight, chain-of-thought monitoring, interpretability, and output review map to Process and Explanation Monitoring and Feedback Acquisition Strategy. Drift, degradation, reward hacking, embedding comparisons, benchmarks, sequential tests, bootstrap procedures, and adversarial evaluation map to Detection Method Selection and Operational Monitoring Signals. Telemetry stacks, dashboards, KPI alerts, and compliance evidence map to Serving Telemetry Integration and Monitoring Artifact Governance. Retraining, continual learning, retrieval augmentation, feedback loops, and update triggers map to Post-Deployment Learning Strategy. Concrete reward-hacking behaviors and distribution-shift failures are outcomes or risks represented by the existing monitoring, integrity, detection, and recovery dimensions rather than new architectural decision axes.

Most codes are covered by existing dimensions: feedback timing, structure, quality, and human oversight fit Feedback Acquisition Strategy; reward design, shaping, hacking, and ambiguity fit Reward Objective Formulation, Reward Shaping and Stabilization, or Reward Mechanism Integrity; trajectory capture, snapshots, versioning, and data lakes fit Monitoring Data Capture and Monitoring Artifact Governance; detection, drift, shadow evaluation, baselines, and statistical diagnostics fit Operational Monitoring Signals, Detection Method Selection, or Policy Rollout Strategy; and guardrails, rollback, and kill switches fit Intervention and Recovery Strategy. The uncovered codes reveal two distinct architectural axes not represented explicitly. First, production serving resource architecture and inference optimization—hardware provisioning, batching, autoscaling, model consolidation, and alignment-preserving compression—governs how monitoring infrastructure meets latency, throughput, cost, and safety constraints; it is not merely a telemetry-integration choice. Second, alert routing and escalation is a monitoring-control decision specifying ownership, urgency, and human escalation paths, which is distinct from selecting signals, detection methods, or recovery actions.

All relevant open codes are subsumed by existing taxonomy dimensions. Runtime shields, static or adaptive safety filters, veto layers, rollback mechanisms, and trigger guards fit Intervention and Recovery Strategy. Offline, shadow, benchmark, counterfactual, trend, slice-based, and ground-truth evaluation fit Production Behavior Evaluation, Reward-Hacking Detection, and Policy Rollout Strategy. State features, intervention rates, domain-specific telemetry, reward/cost signals, dashboards, alert thresholds, routing, deduplication, and burn-rate monitoring fit Operational Signal Collection and Serving Telemetry Integration. Verifier cascades, rubric decomposition, human or AI evaluation, verifier updating, and reward-model disagreement fit Verifier and Supervision Strategy. Reward gating, Lagrangian balancing, conservative objectives, co-optimization, and reward polarity fit Reward Objective Formulation and Reward Shaping and Stabilization. Incident logging, trajectory validation, snapshots, experiment tracking, registries, ingestion checks, and retraining orchestration fit Monitoring Data Capture and Artifact Reproducibility and Governance. RLHF, RLAIF, hybrid feedback, human oversight, feedback quality, and annotation cost fit Feedback Acquisition Strategy. Batch or continual updates, weekly fine-tuning, rehearsal, data mixing, stability-plasticity trade-offs, and post-deployment adaptation fit Post-Deployment Update Strategy. Private-cloud deployment, privacy, compliance, latency, and lifecycle control fit Serving Telemetry Integration and Artifact Reproducibility and Governance. The remaining codes describe monitored failure modes, quality attributes, risks, constraints, or outcomes—such as reward hacking, deceptive generalization, stale safety assumptions, and proxy-goal gaps—rather than introducing an uncovered architectural decision axis.

criteria.name: Clarity

criteria.reason: Most dimensions have recognizable decision scopes and their alternatives are generally distinguishable, especially Detection Method Selection (4), Intervention and Recovery Strategy (5), and Policy Rollout Strategy (7). Reward Objective Design (2) similarly mixes reward formulation with validation and supervision options, so revise its description to cover those existing categories or move values such as 2.16 and 2.14 to the relevant dimensions. Several values are near-duplicates and need more explicit scope distinctions: 1.4 versus 1.13, 6.1 versus 6.19, and 8.5 versus 8.24. Rename or revise their descriptions to state the concrete difference, such as periodic review versus ongoing feedback, conservative offline learning versus generic logged-data learning, and generic experiment tracking versus the MLflow implementation.
